q: A subscription box company offers a plan that costs $18 per month plus a one-time $40 activation fee. A competitor offers a flat $25 per month with no activation fee. After how many full months does the cumulative cost of the first plan first become LESS than the cumulative cost of the competitor's plan?
opts: The first plan is never cheaper
rationale: Set 40 + 18m < 25m, so 40 < 7m, m > 5.71, meaning the first full month where it is cheaper is month 6. At 5 months the first plan costs 130 vs 125 (still more); at 6 it is 148 vs 150 (less). Options 0, 2, 3 mis-handle the threshold or the activation fee.

q: A factory's output of widgets increased by 25% in 2024 over 2023, then decreased by 20% in 2025 from its 2024 level. If 2025 output was 12,000 widgets, what was the 2023 output?
rationale: 2024 = 12,000 / 0.80 = 15,000; 2023 = 15,000 / 1.25 = 12,000. The successive +25% then -20% exactly cancel. Choosing 15,000 (option 4) gives the 2024 figure; 10,800 and 11,200 come from applying the percentages in the wrong direction.

q: Two analysts working together can finish a valuation model in 4 hours. Working alone, the senior analyst would take 6 hours. How long would the junior analyst take to complete the model working alone?
rationale: Combined rate = 1/4 per hour; senior = 1/6 per hour; junior = 1/4 - 1/6 = 1/12, so 12 hours. Option 0 (8) wrongly assumes equal split of the difference; option 4 (2) confuses combined and individual rates.

q: A retailer marks up a jacket 60% above its $50 cost, then runs a promotion taking 30% off the marked price. What is the retailer's profit (or loss) per jacket sold during the promotion?
rationale: Marked price = 50 x 1.6 = 80; sale price = 80 x 0.70 = 56; profit = 56 - 50 = 6. Option 3 ($11) takes 30% off the cost rather than the marked price; option 4 ($24) ignores the discount entirely.

q: A startup's monthly recurring revenue grows according to the compound relationship MRR = 8,000 x (1.05)^n, where n is the number of months elapsed. To the nearest month, after how many months does MRR first exceed $13,000?
rationale: Solve 1.05^n > 13000/8000 = 1.625. ln(1.625)/ln(1.05) = 0.4855/0.0488 = 9.95, so n = 10. Option 0 (8) and option 2 (12) bracket the answer but do not satisfy the inequality at the boundary.

q: A portfolio holds 3 stocks and 2 bonds. A manager will select 2 of the holdings at random to feature in a report. What is the probability that the manager selects exactly one stock and one bond?
rationale: Total ways = C(5,2) = 10. Favorable = 3 x 2 = 6. Probability = 6/10 = 3/5. Note option 3 (6/10) is numerically equal but not reduced; the test convention asks for the reduced form 3/5. Option 1 (2/5) is the complement-style error of choosing two of the same type.

q: Is the average (arithmetic mean) monthly revenue of a 4-store chain greater than $50,000? (1) The total combined revenue of all four stores is $190,000. (2) The store with the highest revenue earns $70,000 per month. Which statement(s) suffice?
opts: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but (2) alone is not
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but (1) alone is not
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but neither alone is
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient
rationale: Mean = total/4. Statement (1) gives total 190,000, so mean = 47,500 < 50,000 — sufficient (answers 'no' definitively). Statement (2) alone fixes only one store and tells nothing about the total, so insufficient. Answer is (1) alone.

q: A box contains red and blue marbles only. What is the probability of drawing a red marble at random? (1) There are 12 blue marbles in the box. (2) The ratio of red to blue marbles is 3 to 2. Which statement(s) suffice?
opts: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but (2) alone is not
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but (1) alone is not
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but neither alone is
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient
rationale: Probability of red = red/(red+blue). Statement (2) alone gives the ratio 3:2, so P(red) = 3/5 directly — sufficient. Statement (1) alone gives only a count of blue with no information on red — insufficient. Answer is (2) alone; the absolute counts are not needed for a probability.

q: A product team runs an A/B test on a new checkout button. The new variant shows a higher conversion rate with a p-value of 0.03 against a pre-registered significance level (alpha) of 0.05. Which interpretation is correct?
opts: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
If the null hypothesis (no difference) were true, there is a 3% chance of observing a result at least this extreme; since 0.03 < 0.05, reject the null
There is a 97% probability the new button is better in the population
The effect size is large because the p-value is small
rationale: A p-value is P(data at least this extreme | null true); 0.03 < 0.05 means reject the null. Option 0 inverts the conditional (the p-value is not the probability the null is true); option 2 misstates it as a confidence in the alternative; option 3 conflates significance with magnitude — a small p-value can accompany a tiny effect.

q: A simple linear regression predicts customer spend (dollars) from email opens: spend = 18 + 2.5(opens), with R-squared = 0.36. Which statement is the most defensible interpretation?
opts: Each additional email open causes $2.50 more spend
36% of the variance in spend is explained by the number of opens, and each additional open is associated with $2.50 more predicted spend
The model correctly predicts spend 36% of the time
A customer with zero opens is predicted to spend $2.50
rationale: R-squared = 0.36 means 36% of variance in the outcome is explained; the slope of 2.5 is an association (predicted change), not necessarily causal. Option 0 overclaims causation from observational regression; option 2 misreads R-squared as accuracy; option 3 confuses the intercept (18) with the slope.

q: A venture fund evaluates a deal: with probability 0.2 it returns 10x the $1M invested, with probability 0.3 it returns 2x, and with probability 0.5 it returns 0. What is the expected net profit on the $1M investment?
rationale: Expected gross return = 0.2(10M) + 0.3(2M) + 0.5(0) = 2M + 0.6M = 2.6M. Net profit = 2.6M - 1M invested = 1.6M. Option 2 ($2.6M) reports gross return without subtracting the investment; option 0 mistakenly nets only against probabilities.

q: A dashboard reports that median order value rose from $42 to $48 while mean order value fell from $61 to $55 over the same quarter. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: The distribution likely became less right-skewed, as very large orders shrank or grew fewer while typical orders rose
The number of orders necessarily decreased
Most customers spent less this quarter than last quarter
rationale: Median up but mean down indicates the right tail (a few very large orders) pulled less, reducing right skew, while the typical (median) order increased. Option 0 and 2 require order counts, which are not given; option 3 contradicts the rising median, which shows the typical customer spent more.
